content_voiceover: This table summarizes the glycoprotein and PAC-1 data across the normal control and two affected family members, labeled here as the patients. Both patients show the same pattern, GPIIb around forty to forty-five percent, GPIIIa around twenty-nine to thirty-one percent, and the critical GPIIb-IIIa dual-positive fraction only seven to ten percent of normal. PAC-1 activation after ADP is similarly blunted in both, eleven to fourteen percent compared to the normal ninety-two percent. Seeing this defect replicated in two family members strongly suggests an inherited, likely autosomal recessive pattern, consistent with Glanzmann thrombasthenia. For boards, the key numeric takeaway is that flow cytometry quantifying GPIIb-IIIa complex expression, not just the individual subunits, is the confirmatory test, and severity roughly correlates with residual expression, type one having less than five percent, type two five to twenty percent, and a variant type having normal expression but a dysfunctional receptor.
keypoints: Both affected relatives: GPIIb/IIIa complex only 7-10% of normal
PAC-1 activation blunted in both (11-14% vs normal 92%)
Concordant findings support an inherited autosomal recessive defect
GT subtypes by residual expression: <5% severe, 5-20% moderate, normal-expression variant type
